html:
The Oyo Empire was a Yoruba state in what is now western Nigeria and eastern Benin, the strongest power between the Niger and the coast in the 1600s and 1700s. The map shows it from 1492 to 1900.

Its king, the Alaafin, ruled from Oyo-Ile, the old capital in the northern savanna. His power was balanced by a council of nobles, the Oyo Mesi, who could force a king who lost their trust to take his own life.

Why it mattered:

  • Horses. Oyo bought horses from the north and built a cavalry that could sweep across open grassland, which made it the military power of the region.
  • Tribute. It made Dahomey pay tribute from the 1730s and controlled the routes to the coast.
  • Trade. Through ports such as Porto-Novo it sold large numbers of captives into the Atlantic slave trade, and much of Yoruba religion and culture travelled with them to Brazil and Cuba.

Oyo culture drew on the older holy city of Ife, which Yoruba tradition sees as the place of creation.

Oyo collapsed in the early 1800s. Its general Afonja rebelled at Ilorin and called in Fulani allies, who brought Ilorin into the Sokoto Caliphate. Oyo-Ile was abandoned in the 1830s, and a new Oyo was built further south. The Yoruba wars that followed fed the slave trade; Samuel Ajayi Crowther was one of the captives. Britain brought the region into its Lagos protectorate in the 1890s, and it later became part of Nigeria.
sum: The Oyo Empire was a Yoruba state in what is now western Nigeria and eastern Benin, the strongest power between the Niger and the coast in the 1600s and 1700s. The map shows it from 1492 to 1900.
